front: Of the three cancer treatment specialties, which give local therapy and which gives systemic therapy?
back: Local: surgical oncology and radiation oncology. Systemic: medical oncology (chemo, immunotherapy, targeted and hormone therapy).
extra: Systemic therapy treats cancer cells (including micrometastases) anywhere in the body. Most patients are planned at a multidisciplinary tumor board.

front: What happens at a CT simulation, and why is it done before planning?
back: The patient is CT-scanned in the exact treatment position with immobilization; that scan is used to contour targets and organs and build the plan, and marks/tattoos let the team reproduce the setup daily.
extra: An isocenter is set at sim as the fixed point the machine targets every day. 4D-CT, contrast, or bladder/rectal preparation are added when motion or anatomy calls for it.

front: What dose per fraction counts as conventional fractionation, and what is hypofractionation?
back: Conventional: about 1.8-2 Gy per fraction. Hypofractionation: fewer fractions with a larger dose per fraction.
extra: Example: 70 Gy in 35 fractions is 2 Gy per fraction; 40 Gy in 15 fractions for breast is hypofractionated.

front: What is redistribution, and why does it help fractionated radiation?
back: Cells are more sensitive to radiation at some points in their growth cycle than others. Cells that survive one fraction may be caught at a more sensitive point by the next one.
extra: For reference: mitosis (M) is the most sensitive phase and late S the most resistant. Redistribution is one of the four R's.

front: Which tissues have a high α/β ratio and which have a low one?
back: High: most tumors and fast-dividing (early-responding) tissues such as skin, mucosa, and marrow. Low: late-responding normal tissues such as the spinal cord, lung, and kidney, and a few tumors, most famously prostate cancer.
extra: Typical values are about 10 (high) and about 3 (low). Low α/β tissues are more sensitive to fraction size, which is why large fractions demand precise aim and why prostate (and breast) cancer can be treated with fewer, larger fractions.

front: What are BED and EQD2 used for?
back: Comparing radiation regimens with different fraction sizes on one scale (EQD2 = the equivalent dose if given in 2 Gy fractions)
extra: BED = nd[1 + d/(α/β)]. Published normal-tissue limits usually assume 2 Gy fractions, so a 1-5 fraction stereotactic plan needs its own limits or a BED/EQD2 conversion, not conventional limits applied directly.

front: What drives acute vs late radiation toxicity?
back: Acute (inflammation, in fast-dividing tissues) depends mainly on total dose over time. Late (fibrosis, months to years later) depends mainly on dose per fraction.
extra: That is why large fractions near late-responding organs demand caution.

front: What is the main way radiation kills cancer cells?
back: DNA damage, especially double-strand breaks, which kill the cell when it tries to divide
extra: Single-strand breaks are easily repaired off the intact opposite strand. Because cells die when they try to divide, tumors shrink over weeks to months, so a scan on the last day of treatment can underestimate the response.

front: How does photon radiation mostly damage DNA?
back: Indirectly: it ionizes water to create free radicals, which then damage DNA.
extra: Oxygen "fixes" this free-radical damage, which is why oxygen matters.

front: What are the four R's of radiobiology that explain why we fractionate?
back: Repair, reoxygenation, repopulation, and redistribution
extra: A fifth R, intrinsic radiosensitivity, is sometimes added.

front: How does hypoxia affect a tumor's response to radiation, and how does fractionation help?
back: Hypoxic cells are more radioresistant. As fractions kill oxygenated cells and the tumor shrinks, hypoxic areas reoxygenate and become more sensitive.
extra: Bulky or necrotic tumors are harder to control partly for this reason. High-LET radiation (neutrons, alpha particles) damages DNA directly and depends much less on oxygen, so its oxygen enhancement ratio falls toward 1.

front: Why can treatment breaks make radiation less effective?
back: Surviving tumor cells keep dividing (repopulation) during gaps in treatment.
extra: Especially important for fast-growing tumors like head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.

front: Do protons automatically give better results than photons?
back: No. Their Bragg peak removes exit dose, which may matter in selected cases (children, craniospinal RT, tumors next to critical structures). Drawbacks: range uncertainty and sensitivity to anatomic change.
extra: Whether the physical dose difference becomes a clinical advantage depends on the disease, the anatomy, and the photon plan it is compared with.

front: Why are deep tumors treated with several photon beams or arcs instead of one?
back: Photons pass through the tumor and keep going (exit dose), so overlapping beams build the highest dose at the tumor while spreading the lower dose across normal tissue.

front: Why might electrons be used instead of photons for a superficial skin lesion?
back: Electrons deposit dose at shallow depth and then fall off quickly, sparing the tissue underneath.
extra: Also used for scar boosts and some shallow nodal targets. The higher the electron energy, the deeper it reaches.

front: What lets protons put most of their dose at a specific depth?
back: The Bragg peak: protons release most of their energy where they stop, with almost no dose beyond.
extra: The depth is set by the beam energy. Several energies are combined into a spread-out Bragg peak (SOBP) to cover the full tumor thickness. Protons are assigned an RBE of 1.1.

front: What is the main difference between external beam radiation and brachytherapy?
back: External beam delivers radiation from a machine outside the patient; brachytherapy places the radioactive source inside or right next to the tumor.
extra: Brachytherapy dose falls off steeply with distance, giving a very high tumor dose while sparing nearby tissue.

front: What do the multileaf collimators (MLCs) in a LINAC do?
back: Their thin metal leaves move to shape the beam to the target and block normal tissue.
extra: Almost every modern technique (3D-CRT, IMRT, VMAT) is a different way of using the MLC.

front: What does IMRT add over 3D-conformal RT, and when is it especially useful?
back: It varies the intensity within each beam so dose can wrap around the target and carve away from nearby organs; useful when the target hugs critical structures (e.g., head and neck).
extra: 3D-CRT uses a few fixed beams with uniform intensity, fine for simple targets and palliation.

front: What is the main difference between IMRT and VMAT?
back: VMAT delivers intensity-modulated treatment while the gantry rotates around the patient.
extra: It is faster to deliver and now one of the most common techniques.

front: What is IGRT, and what is the most common way it is done?
back: Image-guided RT: imaging the patient on the machine before each treatment to confirm position. Usually a cone-beam CT compared with the planning CT.
extra: The tighter the margins, the more IGRT matters. Fiducial markers help for prostate. Cone-beam CT is faster and lower-dose than a diagnostic CT, with poorer image quality, which is enough for alignment.

front: What is the difference between SRS and SBRT?
back: Both deliver very high, precise doses in 1-5 fractions; SRS treats targets in the brain, SBRT targets elsewhere in the body.
extra: Small margins and steep dose falloff mean a few millimeters of error can miss the tumor, so immobilization and image guidance are critical.

front: If splitting the dose protects healthy tissue, why can SRS and SBRT safely give just 1-5 large fractions?
back: The target is small and many beams cross only at the target, so the dose falls off steeply and very little healthy tissue sits in the high-dose region.
extra: This is also why stereotactic treatment demands careful immobilization, motion management, and image guidance: a few millimeters of error matters.

front: What is the difference between LDR and HDR brachytherapy, with a classic example of each?
back: LDR delivers dose slowly over a long time (permanent prostate seeds). HDR sends a high-activity source through an applicator for a few minutes and then removes it (cervical cancer).

front: At a weekly on-treatment visit, why should you look ahead rather than only record how the patient feels today?
back: Radiation side effects build up over the course and often peak at the end of treatment or just after, so a patient who is fine at fraction 5 may be much worse by fraction 20.
extra: Present the fraction number ("fraction 12 of 15"), the side effects and their trend, a focused exam, weight, and the plan. Side effects are graded with CTCAE, for example "grade 1 dermatitis, slightly worse than last week."

front: What four things should a Rad Onc one-liner tell the room?
back: Who the patient is, what cancer they have, how far it has spread (the stage), and why they are here.
extra: Example: "Mr. K is a 64-year-old man with newly diagnosed cT3bN1M0 low rectal adenocarcinoma, referred to us to consider radiation before surgery."

front: When you build a Rad Onc HPI, what question decides whether a detail belongs in it?
back: Would this fact change the diagnosis, the stage, the treatment, or radiation safety? If not, it probably does not belong.
extra: Always include prior radiation (site, dose, and when) and radiation-safety issues such as connective tissue disease, IBD before pelvic RT, or a pacemaker.

front: What is the difference between neoadjuvant and adjuvant therapy?
back: Neoadjuvant is given before the main treatment (e.g., to shrink a tumor before surgery); adjuvant is given after it to lower the risk of recurrence.
extra: Always ask what the intent of this specific treatment is; one patient's plan can include both.

front: What does it mean when radiation is called "definitive"?
back: It is intended to be the complete, final treatment, with no further therapy planned to finish the job (e.g., definitive chemoradiation instead of surgery).
extra: Curative describes the goal (cure); definitive describes the role of the treatment.

front: Why is chemotherapy often given concurrently with radiation?
back: It sensitizes the tumor to radiation (and treats disease outside the field).
extra: Classic examples: cisplatin with head and neck or cervical RT.

front: What is the goal of palliative radiation, and what are classic reasons to give it?
back: Symptom relief in incurable disease, e.g., painful bone metastases, spinal cord compression, bleeding, airway obstruction, or SVC syndrome
extra: Palliative courses are usually short, chosen by prognosis and goals of care.

front: What is the role of radiation in oligometastatic disease?
back: Focused high-dose RT (usually SBRT/SRS) to the few sites of metastatic disease to control them, often alongside systemic therapy
extra: It can delay progression or the need to change systemic therapy.

front: What is consolidative radiation?
back: RT given after another treatment modality, usually chemotherapy, to improve control of the disease that remains (e.g., residual bulky lymphoma).
extra: Name the intent before the dose: it decides how much toxicity is acceptable and how aggressive the plan is.

front: Why is smoking cessation addressed with essentially every radiation patient?
back: Smoking during radiation lowers tumor control and worsens side effects (tissue hypoxia makes tumors more radioresistant and slows healing).
extra: Other "do not forget" items for a new patient: fertility counseling before gonadal exposure, a pregnancy test when relevant, genetic counseling when a hereditary syndrome is suspected, and performance status.

front: As a first way of thinking about dose limits, how do "serial" and "parallel" organs differ?
back: Serial-type organs (spinal cord, brainstem, optic pathway) can lose function from a small high-dose region, so the maximum dose gets attention. Parallel-type organs (lung, liver, kidney, parotid) can tolerate a small hot region if enough of the organ is spared, so mean dose or volume matters.
extra: A teaching simplification: many organs behave partly both ways, and the actual limits are site- and protocol-specific.

front: What does a constraint like "lung V20 < 30%" mean?
back: Less than 30% of the lung volume should receive 20 Gy or more.
extra: The number itself depends on the protocol and the situation. Dmax (or D0.03cc) is the maximum dose; D90 is the dose that 90% of a volume receives.

front: What is the standard spinal cord maximum dose with conventional fractionation?
back: About 50 Gy
extra: Myelopathy risk is tiny at 50 Gy but rises steeply above it.

front: With conventional fractionation, what maximum dose is used for the brainstem and optic nerves/chiasm?
back: About 54-55 Gy
extra: Exceeding these risks brainstem necrosis or blindness.

front: What is the difference between a sequential boost and a simultaneous integrated boost (SIB)?
back: Sequential ("cone down"): treat the large volume first, then a separate phase treats only the boost volume. SIB: both volumes are treated every day in one phase, at different doses per fraction.

front: What do the nested target volumes GTV, CTV, ITV, and PTV each add?
back: GTV = visible tumor. CTV adds microscopic spread. ITV adds internal motion (e.g., breathing). PTV adds daily setup uncertainty.
extra: The PTV is usually the volume that gets the prescription. Not every case uses every layer. A PRV (planning risk volume) is the OAR version of a PTV: an organ at risk plus a margin, used around serial structures like the spinal cord.

front: Why is a CTV usually skipped for a brain metastasis or vestibular schwannoma?
back: These lesions are well defined and do not infiltrate microscopically, so the GTV goes straight to a PTV.

front: Why is there usually no separate GTV for prostate cancer?
back: The cancer is usually microscopic or multifocal and not reliably seen, so the whole prostate (± seminal vesicles) is contoured as the CTV.

front: In plan review, what is the difference between coverage and conformity?
back: Coverage asks whether the whole target (including its edges) gets the prescribed dose; conformity asks how tightly the high-dose region hugs the target.
extra: A good plan covers the target while sparing everything else.

front: When is a hotspot in a radiation plan acceptable, and when is it a problem?
back: A small hotspot inside the tumor is usually fine; one inside an organ at risk (e.g., the spinal cord) is not.

front: A target touches the spinal cord, and full coverage would exceed the cord limit. What does the plan usually give up?
back: A little coverage at the edge of the target next to the cord. The cord limit is respected even if that edge gets slightly less than the prescribed dose.
extra: A good plan fully treats the target while keeping side effects acceptable; when the two conflict, the doctor decides. The same logic drives ultracentral lung SBRT, where airway limits can win over full PTV coverage.

front: What does a dose-volume histogram (DVH) show?
back: What percentage of a structure's volume receives at least each dose
extra: It lets you check every target and organ at risk against its limits without scrolling through every slice.

front: Why is a DVH not enough on its own to judge a plan?
back: It shows how much dose each structure receives, not where; hotspots and coverage gaps must be checked on the isodose lines slice by slice.

front: What does the plan-review checklist CB-CHOP stand for?
back: Contours, Beams, Coverage, Hotspots, OARs, Prescription
extra: It is the order an attending runs through a plan on the screen.

front: In the plan at the end of a Rad Onc presentation, what should you address before naming a dose?
back: The patient's goals and preferences, and the intent (cure or relief).
extra: Then give a dose and number of fractions, your reasoning and the trial behind it, the surgery and systemic therapy around the radiation, and any patient-specific risks.

front: At a consult, what should you ask before explaining the patient's cancer?
back: What they already know: what their other doctors have told them so far.
extra: Then use ask, tell, ask: explain one piece in plain words, check what they took from it, and repeat.

front: What is teach-back?
back: Asking the patient to explain the plan back in their own words, to check how well you explained it.
extra: Use it at the end of the visit, for example: "Can you tell me in your own words what the next steps are?"

front: A patient receiving external beam radiation asks whether they will be radioactive around their grandchildren. What is the answer?
back: No. The radiation is on only while the machine runs, and nothing stays in the body.
extra: Some brachytherapy implants, such as permanent prostate seeds, come with specific precautions.

front: For a target, what is the difference between D95% and V95%?
back: D95% is the dose that 95% of the target receives. V95% is the percentage of the target that receives at least 95% of the prescribed dose.
extra: Both describe coverage from the same DVH curve: D asks what dose a given volume gets, V asks how much volume gets a given dose.

front: What is DIBH, and why is it used for left-sided breast radiation?
back: Deep inspiration breath hold: treating only while the patient holds a deep breath, which moves the heart away from the field and lowers heart dose.
extra: Late heart risk rises with the average heart dose.

front: How does adaptive radiation therapy differ from IGRT?
back: IGRT moves the patient to match the plan. Adaptive therapy changes the plan itself when the anatomy has changed, such as after major weight loss or tumor shrinkage.

front: Why can a standard spinal cord limit be unsafe for a plan that re-treats the same area?
back: The cord already received dose from the first course, so the limit has to apply to the total (cumulative) dose.
extra: Re-treatment needs the old plan, the time since it was given, and stricter limits.
